notes: Case stated appeal on racially aggravated assault; DPP v M governs 'foreigner' language.

enrichment.short_title: DPP v Balham Youth Court: racially aggravated assault and 'foreigner' hostility
key_facts: The DPP appealed after Balham Youth Court upheld no case to answer on a charge of racially aggravated assault against B.
The Crown case was that B punched Abdel Djemal after calling him a 'fucking foreigner' and threatening that foreigners should 'die', having earlier brandished a knife in a takeaway dispute.
The district judge held the word 'foreigner' did not fall within section 28 and that the prosecution had not proved racial hostility.
B had separately been convicted of ABH in April 2003 and sentenced to a six-month detention and training order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by case stated against a youth court decision upholding a submission of no case to answer.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the youth court decision was quashed and the case remitted to a differently designated district judge.
enrichment.ratio: Following DPP v M, abusive use of 'foreigner' in the immediate context of an assault can demonstrate hostility based on presumed membership of a racial group for section 28 purposes; a relevant statutory misconstruction is grounds to remit even where later authority clarifies the law.
legal_issues: Whether 'foreigner' language is capable of demonstrating racial hostility under section 28
Whether the youth court erred in upholding no case to answer
Whether autrefois acquit barred remittal after a successful no-case submission
Whether the case should be remitted despite delay and B's separate ABH conviction
linked_authorities: Director of Public Prosecutions v M (a Minor) [2004] EWHC 1453 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Statutory analysis, factual summary and remittal order are clearly recorded.

notes: SEND tribunal appeal on autism statement; sleep and safety issues analysed in detail.

enrichment.short_title: W v Leeds: special educational needs statement for autistic child
key_facts: The mother appealed a SEND tribunal decision dismissing her challenge to Leeds City Council's statement for her nine-year-old autistic son, C.
C had significant communication, toileting, feeding and social interaction difficulties requiring specialist provision.
The tribunal excluded from Part 2 a reference to sleeping difficulties leading to aggression, and declined to specify overnight supervision at school.
The mother argued the tribunal had wrongly treated sleep-related safety needs as non-educational and had procedurally prejudiced her case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Administrative Court from a Special Educational Needs and Disability Tribunal decision under section 326 of the Education Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the tribunal's reasoning on sleep-related needs and absence of material prejudice was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Overnight supervision required only for safety reasons, where sleep behaviour cannot be taught and does not act as a barrier to learning at school, does not constitute a special educational need warranting statement provision.
legal_issues: Whether sleep-related safety and aggression should have been specified in the statement
Whether the tribunal erred in excluding paragraph 9(b) from Part 2
Whether the mother suffered material prejudice from the way the sleep issue was raised
Whether the statement adequately addressed C's autism-related educational needs

confidence.notes: Factual background and dismissal on sleep-related reasoning are clearly stated.

notes: Highly unusual Sudan/England child abduction and Schedule 1 jurisdiction case.

enrichment.short_title: Re S: Schedule 1 jurisdiction after unlawful retention of habitually resident child
key_facts: Sudanese parents married in 1996; their child M was born in England in 1998 and found habitually resident here.
After divorce under Sudanese law the father unlawfully retained M in Sudan at the end of contact in September 2001.
The mother sought financial provision under Schedule 1 and injunctive relief over the former matrimonial home in London.
Bracewell J declined jurisdiction and refused permission to appeal; Kirkwood J had held M remained habitually resident in England.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Permission and substantive appeal against refusal of a Schedule 1 Children Act 1989 application for want of jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the Schedule 1 application was restored to be heard on its merits and injunctive relief over the property continued.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 14 of Schedule 1 is not a comprehensive jurisdictional code excluding all other cases; jurisdiction may exist where a child is habitually resident in England but absent because of unlawful retention abroad by the other parent.
legal_issues: Whether the court had jurisdiction to entertain a Schedule 1 application
Whether paragraph 14 of Schedule 1 excluded applications where the child was not present in England
Whether the mother's claim was essentially for her own benefit rather than for the child
Whether injunctive relief over the matrimonial home should continue pending merits hearing
linked_authorities: Re Halsted's Will Trusts [1937] 2 All ER 570

confidence.notes: Unusual facts and explicit appellate restoration of the Schedule 1 application are clearly recorded.

notes: Long animal-rights protest injunction hearing; exclusion zones upheld as proportionate.

enrichment.short_title: Oxford University v Broughton: protest injunction and exclusion zones
key_facts: Oxford University and related claimants sought continuation of injunctive relief against animal-rights protesters opposing construction of a research laboratory.
Defendants included SPEAK campaigners and individuals with histories of aggravated trespass and serious criminal convictions.
Ex parte and interim orders had already been made by Cox J and Simon J restricting protest activity near protected persons and sites.
Some defendants gave undertakings or were no longer actively targeted; SPEAC's continuation was refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application to continue representative injunctive relief against animal-rights protesters.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction largely continued in Simon J's terms, incorporating additional prohibitions including photography of protected persons; costs reserved.
enrichment.ratio: Where repeated protest activity would amount to harassment if directed at individuals, representative injunctive relief with defined exclusion zones and a photography ban may be necessary and proportionate to protect lawful construction work.
legal_issues: Whether continuation of the injunction against each defendant was justified
Whether exclusion zones were necessary and proportionate
Whether a prohibition on photographing protected persons should be included
Whether representative proceedings under CPR 19.6 were appropriate

confidence.notes: Core proportionality reasoning and final order variations are clearly stated.

notes: Leave to remove refused after five-day welfare hearing; mother's instability central.

enrichment.short_title: Re R: refusal of permanent relocation of young children to Paris
key_facts: The mother sought a residence order and permission permanently to remove two very young children to live with her in Paris.
She argued she was isolated and unhappy in London and would receive better support from her French family.
The father opposed removal and sought joint residence if any residence order were made.
After a five-day hearing the judge found the mother's emotional instability and impulsiveness made relocation contrary to the children's welfare.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application for residence and leave permanently to remove children from the jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to remove refused; residence granted to the mother as main carer and existing contact arrangements largely continued with minor timing adjustments.
enrichment.ratio: In relocation cases the children's welfare is paramount; a parent's unhappiness and wish for a fresh start cannot justify permanent removal where instability and the risk that relocation will not succeed outweigh the benefits.
legal_issues: Whether the children should be permitted to live permanently in Paris
Whether a residence order should be made and in what form
Whether the father's objection was punitive or welfare-based
What contact arrangements best served the children's interests

confidence.notes: Welfare findings, refusal of relocation and residence/contact orders are explicit.

notes: TCC privilege ruling on Soilfrac supermarket defects claim and insurer advice.

enrichment.short_title: Sainsbury v WSP: disclosure of Pepper report and partial privilege waiver
key_facts: Sainsbury claimed against WSP over defective ground-bearing slab design at a Newhaven supermarket later treated by Soilfrac grouting.
WSP sought disclosure of three classes of documents including collateral legal advice and an expert report by Mr Pepper.
Sainsbury had deployed redacted documents at trial, partially waiving privilege over decision-making on abandoning further grouting.
The Pepper report was obtained while Sainsbury and its insurers had opposing interests in a buildings insurance claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court interlocutory application for disclosure during trial of engineering negligence claim.
enrichment.outcome: Mr Pepper's report was ordered to be disclosed; redacted material also had to be disclosed to ensure fairness where privilege had been partially waived.
enrichment.ratio: Common interest privilege requires substantially the same interest at the time advice is given; advice obtained while insurer and insured are in dispute over a policy claim does not become privileged merely because their interests later align.
legal_issues: Whether partial deployment of redacted documents required disclosure of withheld passages
Whether Mr Pepper's report attracted common interest privilege
Whether collateral legal advice had to be disclosed
What fairness required where claimants relied on selected privileged material at trial
linked_authorities: Great Atlantic Insurance Co v Home Insurance Co (The Good Luck) [1991] 1 WLR 117
Ventouris v Mountain (The Italia Express) (No 2) [1991] 1 WLR 607

confidence.notes: Privilege reasoning on the Pepper report and partial waiver is clearly explained.

notes: Without-prejudice patent letter treated as invitation to negotiate; action struck out.

enrichment.short_title: Schering v Cipla: strike-out of patent claim based on without-prejudice letter
key_facts: Schering sued Cipla and Neolab for threatened infringement of patent EP (UK) 0152897 relating to desloratadine.
The sole pleaded infringement was a 6 July 2004 'without prejudice' letter stating Cipla's intention to launch generic products and inviting commercial discussions.
Cipla argued the letter was privileged and did not constitute a threat or act of infringement.
Schering had obtained permission to serve the claim out of the jurisdiction rather than entering negotiations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery Division application to strike out patent infringement proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted; the action was struck out because the letter was protected by without-prejudice privilege and could not support the particulars of infringement.
enrichment.ratio: A without-prejudice letter asserting patent invalidity while inviting an acceptable commercial solution is a negotiating document and cannot be relied on as evidence of threatened infringement.
legal_issues: Whether Cipla's letter amounted to a threat of patent infringement
Whether the letter was protected by without prejudice privilege
Whether the claim should be struck out as disclosing no reasonable cause of action
Whether service out of the jurisdiction had been properly obtained

confidence.notes: Single-document strike-out reasoning and privilege conclusion are direct and unambiguous.

notes: Committal sentence appeal; concurrent and consecutive structure adjusted.

enrichment.short_title: Salih v Sharif: appeal against committal sentence for breach of non-molestation order
key_facts: Mr Salih was committed to 18 months' imprisonment for four breaches of a county court non-molestation order.
The breaches included harassment at his wife's home, school and workplace over several days in August 2004.
He appealed sentence only, appearing in person after public funding was withdrawn shortly before the hearing.
The breaches followed a history of alleged domestic violence and separation in March 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence in committal proceedings for breach of a family injunction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; total sentence reduced from 18 months to 12 months by restructuring concurrent and consecutive terms.
enrichment.ratio: Breaches occurring in a short connected sequence should ordinarily be sentenced concurrently, with any later distinct breach sentenced consecutively; total committal must remain proportionate.
legal_issues: Whether the overall 18-month committal sentence was disproportionate
Whether breaches on consecutive days should have been treated as one course of conduct
Whether the appeal should be entertained despite slight delay and lack of representation
How concurrent and consecutive sentences should be structured for multiple breaches

confidence.notes: Sentence structure and partial allowance of appeal are clearly explained.

notes: Section 69/68 challenge to arbitrator's costs award after misdescribed dispute.

enrichment.short_title: Newfield v Tomlinson: challenge to arbitrator's costs award under the 1996 Act
key_facts: Newfield bought the Tomlinsons' house as part of a profit-sharing development at Ribble Point, Lytham St Annes.
A partial award declared the meaning of profit-sharing clauses; the arbitrator awarded costs to the Tomlinsons as the successful party.
Newfield argued the arbitrator misunderstood the dispute because both sides' cases turned on forecast sale value, not actual sales.
The arbitrator's later correspondence acknowledged that but for his error the costs award would have been reversed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court applications under sections 69 and 68 of the Arbitration Act 1996 to challenge an arbitrator's costs award.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to appeal granted and appeal allowed under section 69; the costs award was varied so the Tomlinsons pay Newfield's recoverable arbitration costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where an arbitrator materially misdescribes the dispute before him and awards costs on that mistaken basis, section 69 may be satisfied and the error may also amount to a serious irregularity causing substantial injustice under section 68.
legal_issues: Whether the arbitrator erred in law in identifying the parties' cases on developer's margin
Whether the costs award could be challenged under section 69
Whether there was a serious irregularity under section 68(2)(c)
Whether substantial injustice was caused by the misdescription of the dispute
linked_authorities: Fence Gate Ltd v NEL Construction Ltd [2000] BLR 496

confidence.notes: Arbitrator's admitted error and variation of the costs award are clearly documented.

notes: Article 81 illegality defence on damages inquiry; cause of action estoppel rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Blackburn v Bim Kemi: Article 81 defence after stayed competition issues
key_facts: Blackburn and Bim disputed a 1994 sourcing and exclusivity agreement for antifoam and lint-control products.
The Court of Appeal held Bim repudiated the contract and Blackburn was entitled to damages, but competition-law issues had been stayed.
After Blackburn abandoned its own Article 81 plea, Bim sought to rely on illegality to resist assessment of Blackburn's counterclaim.
Cooke J allowed Bim to raise the point; Blackburn appealed on cause of action estoppel grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal to strike out Bim's Article 81 illegality defence on assessment of damages.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Bim remained entitled to argue that the 1994 agreement was void for Article 81 illegality.
enrichment.ratio: A stay of competition issues and a conditional Court of Appeal judgment did not create cause of action estoppel; where Blackburn first raised and later abandoned the illegality plea, it was not an abuse for Bim to rely on the same point after losing on liability.
legal_issues: Whether cause of action estoppel prevented Bim from raising Article 81 illegality
Whether the Henderson v Henderson abuse of process principle applied
Whether the court must consider manifest illegality despite estoppel arguments
Effect of Langley J's stay and the Court of Appeal's 24 June 2003 order
linked_authorities: Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 2 AC 59
Co-Flexip SA v Stolt Offshore MS Ltd [2004] FSR 708
Arnold v National Westminster Bank [1991] 2 AC 93

confidence.notes: Detailed procedural history and explicit dismissal on estoppel grounds are clearly recorded.
